projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Victor W. McIntire was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Victor W. McIntire. Mr. McIntire served in the U.S. Navy with the Seabees. He served in the Pacific Theater, and his highest rank was Machinist Mate Third Class. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded on January 7, 2005 at Mr. McIntire's home in East Lake, Ohio. Victor was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: In 1941, I was living in Wellsville, Ohio where I was born and raised. I graduated from high school there in 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In '43. So that would have made you, what, about 15 in 1941?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah, I think 16.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sixteen?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah, about 16.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah, I do. I was driving my uncle and his wife and an aunt of mine from Akron to Wellsville. Our high school basketball team had played Akron Garfield, and the coach allowed me to stay over in Akron with my in-laws, or my uncle and aunt, because they were planning to drive to Wellsville on Sunday. My uncle was a policeman in Akron, and he had a new 1941 Chevrolet car. And I had been driving since I was 13, so -- and the two ladies could not drive. So I'm driving; and he had been on the night turn, so he is in the back seat asleep. The chance to drive a new car with a radio in it -- We had the radio on and, lo and behold, during that trip, the news came on that Pearl Harbor had been bombed. So that was something I will always remember, that recollection, getting to drive that new Chevrolet car and listening to the radio. That was my first recollection.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Well, at the time -- I don't recall exactly what it was. I guess, I am 16 years old, and I knew it was serious; and I knew from the reaction of the two aunts and the uncle -- of course, he was asleep, so I don't think he picked up on it right away -- that this was a serious situation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was school like that next day when you went in?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: I can't remember much about that, about what the reaction to school was. I imagine there were a number of people who hadn't picked up on it because, you know, I guess everyone had radios, or a lot of people had radios. Of course, they had no television or anything like that. But it was just a news item. I don't think they had grasped exactly how serious it was because it took a few days, I guess, for the damage to become apparent to everyone, you know, to really get word back from Pearl Harbor as to just exactly what had happened and how serious it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you -- Did they have you listen to FDR's speech on that day?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yes, I have heard that, day that lives in infamy, the fact that we had been -- a group had bombed our Naval base at Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any of your classmates decide to get out and sign up?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: A lot of them did. Wellsville is a small town, probably at that time, maybe, five, 6,000 people. But a river town, typical little river town. And many, many young men volunteered immediately, like they did all over the country. And, in fact, once I -- well, when I was still in high school, a senior in high school, I tried to volunteer. And there was an aviation cadet program at that time. And when it first started, they wanted college graduates to be pilots and so on. And this was before the Air Force became a separate branch of the military. It was part of the Army Air Force, they called it. And I went to Pittsburgh and took the physical and the mental -- or the written test. And I had a little stigmatism in my right eye and, consequently, that -- that defeated me. Being a kid at that nature, well, my brother and I were kind of airplane nuts, and the airplane was still kind of a, somewhat of a novelty. And, of course, everybody wanted to be in the Air Force. So then, we just waited. And the draft boards worked rather diligently in those days. You didn't have to wait long. I think we had to sign up when we were 17, if I am not -- When you turned 18, you were eligible then, and they could pull your number out of the pot or out of the hat, whatever they used. But after I missed that opportunity, why, some of the fellows I went with, they were -- they passed. I passed the written test, and rather easily. In fact, the fellow that ran the operation called me in and said, "We are going to let you go ahead and take the physical again." He said, normally, the eye test was the first thing they -- first thing you got. And I remember a couple of the doctors or the testers getting together, and one fellow who was the guy in charge says, "Okay, well, let him go ahead. Let him take the rest of the physical." So, that was kind of an experience in the old Post Office building or something in Pittsburgh. And standing around naked, big long lines, going from one doctor to another, being a kid, kids were not quite used to that. But having participated in football and everything else, why, it was nothing unusual. But I did take -- and they called me in after the physical exam was completed. And there were a couple of fellows there, and they said, "Well, your written score was so high that we were going to take another check," he said, "but the standards won't let us accept you with that impairment." So I just went back home and waited for the draft board to do its thing, which it did. And it took awhile because I think what happened in those days, draft boards had to meet a quota. And every county had a draft board made up of citizens. And if a lot of fellows were volunteering, they met their quota through the guys who volunteered, and that kind of delayed things. But we had to tell them, the draft board, ahead of time what we were going to do so they wouldn't be pulling us out of there unnecessarily. But then, once you -- if you didn't make it, you had to go back and tell them, "Well, put me back in there," which they did, of course. That's how I ended up. We at that time then, when the draft board operated, we went over to Lisbon, which is the county seat. And there were three busloads the day I reported. I was still 18. And we had three full busloads that went from Columbiana County up to Cleveland. We came up to Cleveland to go through the physical again. And then the various branches of the service would come through and try to talk you into going with them. And you had a choice. You had a little bit of a choice. I was with another fellow from my class. And the draft, of course, wasn't, physically, wasn't quite as strict as they were with the Air Force aviation program. I learned later that a fellow said, "Well, heck, if you would have gone to the Navy, they would have taken you." I said, "Holy --" and, but that's -- they had Marines and Air Force, but not Air Force guys as much as Navy and Army guys there. And they were going along through the line, and they had all your papers there. And they were trying to talk guys into getting in the Marine Corps, or "Do you want to go to the Army? You want to go to --" I don't recall as I reacted very well. One fellow says, "Hey, come on. Come on with me." I guess he probably saw in there that I had some mechanical training, like I had gone to a vocational school while I was in high school to learn to be a machinist, and that probably was on there. So I ended up in the Seabees because they were needing young fellows at that time. The Seabees, basically, were a bunch of older men who were construction workers and heavy equipment operators and had been over there in the Pacific and kind of got caught over there; but the jobs they did were needed. So the Navy, I guess, just decided, well, we might as well have our own instead of having these civilian guys over here doing it. So, that's how I ended up in the Seabees. "Why don't you come with me?" So I did. Me and the fellow that I was with, we were together, so we went along. I have often thought about that. Standing in that line, the fellow in front of me and the fellow behind me, both from my high school class, were both killed, one in Italy and one in the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They went in the Army then?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah, they both went into the Army. And, boy, I thought of that -- I thought of that many times in my lifetime that, gee, those two guys, they -- why I got picked to go to the Navy or picked myself, I guess. The guy says, "Come on with me," and I did. The Navy guys all went here, and the Marines went there, and the Army guys went somewhere else. After the physical, they marched us off to dinner somewhere, to probably -- I don't know whether -- can't remember exactly, but I remember walking through the streets of Cleveland from the old Post Office building to a restaurant. It might have been the Forum Restaurant. I don't know. It used to be down there on Ninth Street. It was a cafeteria. I am not sure of that, but I remember marching through the streets. And then we went down and got on a train down under the terminal tower there; and some went one way, and some went another. I remember that. We happened to be lucky enough to get a Pullman car. That didn't happen too often. But we traveled during the night and all the next day. And the next evening, rather late, we ended up in Williamsburg, Virginia at Camp Perry, which was one of the early Seabee bases. I think there were probably two in the country at that time, one up in Rhode Island and one in Williamsburg. And I don't know whether the one in Gulfport was in operation or not yet down on the gulf coast. But we ended up in Williamsburg. I will never forget that. For a kid who had never been away from home before, it was quite a sight. We get there rather late at night, and the old steam engine and looking out the windows of the train, floodlights all over the place and hundreds of guys milling around outside there, and the steam from the engine and the lights and the yelling and hollering and guys coming through and reading off your name; and you trumped out. The guys reading off the names couldn't pronounce half of them, so you didn't know whether they were calling you or not. And McIntire doesn't always easy to pronounce. I got McInerny and got all kinds of different names. But I learned to know what they were talking about or who they were calling for. So we ended up in Williamsburg, Virginia. That's where we did what they call the Navy boot camp. We were there, I was, in October.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: October of '43?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it the same boot camp that the other Navy people were to go through?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: No. It was strictly the Seabee base for the Naval Construction Battalion. Others went to Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What I mean, as far as the training, was the training the same?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: The training -- they taught you all the Naval, Navy protocol and all that sort of thing; but then much of the training was done by the Marine Corps, which was kind of infantry training. We got a lot of the boot training was much infantry training where you got -- And then we had some -- had six weeks of that and then six weeks of what they called advanced training where we were on rifle ranges, and we were taught infantry stuff, how to use grenades and machine guns and bayonets and all of the various things because Camp Lejeune and Cherry Point, those places were just down the road, so there were a lot of Marines on the base. And they conducted much of the advanced training. The Naval protocol was done by Navy personnel. But there were a lot of -- a lot of older men, men who had trades and that sort of thing. Heck, one of my bunkmates was a fellow who had been the mayor of Little Falls, New York. And he was a newspaper man. He had about as much reason to be there as the man in the moon. He was a heck of a nice guy, but he just -- he was probably in his late thirties. But all the young guys, the 18-year olds, they had it -- we were all mixed together. We had -- we all did the same boot camp together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any of the older guys have any trouble going through that?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Oh, yeah, a lot of them. J. B. McGuire, when we did the 20-mile hike, I carried his rifle and his pack and everything else. I remember him saying to me, "Boy, Mac, hadn't been for you, I would have never got through this." He had bad feet, and he was not a fellow here. Heck, here was an 18-year old kid who was as strong as a mule, you know, played a lot of football and stuff. And it was -- plus, I liked the guy. He was real nice. He was a gentleman. There were fellows of all -- all vocations in there, carpenters, electricians, draftsmen, heavy equipment operators, powder men from up in Minnesota, guys from the iron ore mines up there. And then they -- that summer then, they loaded us all on trains and sent us up to Rhode Island. There was a Naval -- or a Seabee base up there in Davisville, Rhode Island. That's just south of Providence, right down on Narraganset Bay. Providence is right up at the head of Narraganset Bay, and Davisville is about halfway down. And it was more of an advanced training place. And that's where they made up battalions. They just took these trainloads of guys from the summertime. I will never forget that. Camp Perry in the winter was colder than the Dickens. We were down there in the swamp of Virginia, and it was -- it was pretty nippy. But we did some -- We got some building where you went out and built some -- these air strips for the Navy, the landing strips, emergency landing strips. We built a couple of those, mainly for practice to learn how to do it. They put those steel mats down that the Navy planes could land on and the Marines. And we did some invasion landing. They loaded us in landing craft and took us out on the Chesapeake Bay or the James River, and we had to come ashore and act like we were attacking somebody. So that was part of that infantry training, of course. But up in Davisville, they put us into battalions. And that particular base at that time, they were making what they called special battalions. All them Seabee battalions were maybe a thousand men to a battalion. And a lot of them had special jobs that they did. They were road builders, or they were airfield builders, or they just built moors and docks. And some of them -- and our particular specialty as as a special battalion was in stevedoring, handling cargo and that sort of thing. They had some, what they called, dry land ships. It looked like a ship, but it was just a deck of the ship. And they had the booms and winches and all of that, and we learned there how to operate that equipment, the winches and that sort of thing, because we had a lot of men who were in the stevedore business in New York City and the gulf ports in New Orleans and Galveston and those places down on the gulf coast. And they were older men, of course. But the young fellows, guys like myself, why, we had to learn to do that sort of thing; and they were kind of the teachers, yet some of them stayed in the battalions with us. We spent a summer there. And that summer, late that summer, maybe July or August, after the battalions were made up, and we did some other special work there. I remember I had to go to a school for drafting and map making, making topographical maps. We learned that that would be used for invasion purposes, you know. Or you would take transit readings from, who were the guys with the surveys, and make these into maps so that guys could read maps and know what the height of the elevation of the ground and so on was. I had to go to that school, and then I had to go to 30 caliber machine gun school. And I got to go to the rifle range. We all had carbines, but I got to know the BAR, the Browning Automatic Rifle, and that sort of thing. You had to learn to take them apart and, you know, put them together and field strip them, as they called it. And we spent that summer there in Davisville. Camp Endicott, it was called. Today it's pretty much gone. And Williamsburg, Camp Perry in Williamsburg, is now a CIA base. That's -- we tried to go back and visit it one time when we were in Virginia and couldn't get near it. They run a superhighway down right in front of it, like one of our interstates. But you you couldn't get on the base. It was heavily guarded. I thought it would be nice to go back and just see if I remembered anything, but it wasn't about to happen. But they loaded us on trains, and we traveled across the country, took about a week to go from Davisville, Rhode Island. We road out to -- went out to California, up in the hills above Oakland there at Stockton. And what the heck was the other place? But there was a base there; and we stayed there for maybe a week or so, and then they shipped us down into Oakland. And we lived in a little, kind of an emergency camp right in Oakland. Well, it wasn't in Oakland, actually. It was in a little town called Emoryville, between Berkeley and Oakland, right on the main road that ran along the bay there. And we lived there, and went over to the Naval supply depot and actually got hands-on experience on real ships loading all kinds of Naval cargo ships. Anything that needed -- that the Navy would need in the Pacific was pretty much there. We spent -- we were there from August, maybe, until January sometime. And while we were there, we talked our chaplain into helping us organize a football team. Well, that really struck a note with guys like myself and all these ex-high school kids who had played football and still thought they could. And he was a rather jovial, cooperative guy. And he, some way or other, he makes arrangements with Santa Clara, the college out there; and they gave us a whole bunch of old, used football equipment, helmets, shoulder pads, all the pads and stuff, pants, shoes, everything, stuff that they didn't want. Of course, I don't think they had a football program at that time. Many of the colleges had abandoned their football programs. Some of the bigger ones still continued to. University of California was right there in Berkeley, and we could go up there. But we organized a football team, and we found out we had some kids who could really play. And I don't know whether or not, but we had a chief that was supposed to be the coach, but I don't think he knew a heck of a lot about it. But we were able to play six or eight games. We played University of California freshman team in its preliminary games before their varsity games on a Saturday morning. We played them twice. Camp Beale was up in Sacramento, and they were a really good, well organized team. They had been playing for a couple years. In fact, the year after we played them, they won the National Service Championship. It was probably 1944. And we played a black Air Force team up in Marysville, a fighter squadron. And then we played the landing force team in Richmond, California. They had a landing force base up there. We played Hollister Junior College, and they were hotter than the Dickens. We played a number of games. It was a great experience. Then from there, they shipped us down to Port Hueneme. It was in Oxnard, California, down there just below Ventura and just up the valley from Los Angeles. And we were there then through January and, I think, into February before they shipped us out. That was a big advance base depot for the Navy. They had all kinds of equipment there. Anything that they would need in the Pacific could be shipped out of Port Hueneme. And we spent some time there until they get -- I guess until they decided what to do with us or where they needed us, where they wanted us. Finally, a ship came in and they said, well, you better make your -- get your ducks in a row, because you are going to -- we're going to be shipping out of here. We had no idea where we are going. Of course, things at that time -- there was still a lot of fighting going on in Luzon up in the upper part of the Philippines because the return invasion of the Philippines had happened in October, but that was down in the Leyte area down toward the middle part of the Philippines, Leyte/Samar area. And, lo and behold, that's where we ended up. But we boarded an old ship that the Navy had confiscated over in East Indies over in there, Burma or somewhere, and it belonged to the Dutch East Indies Steamship Company. It was nothing more than an old cargo vessel, and they had converted it into a troop ship. And we loaded aboard that thing, and we had our battalion and a half of a black battalion with us. They occupied the three holds which were converted into sleeping quarters in the back of the ship, and we had the three holds to the front. And we disembarked from Port Hueneme and spent 40 days sailing across the Pacific, went from Port Hueneme to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Well, I will never forget the first -- right off the coast of California, there is what they call the Japanese currents. They come travel southward, kind of like the east coast -- what's it called on the east coast? Anyway, they are quite rough. There is an area there of heavy water. And, lo and behold, there was some seasickness. And I was included. I will never forget that. That first day out, we must have sailed around 2:30 in the afternoon. We spent all the day before loading up and getting everything, then they marched us aboard and assigned us to a bunk, and so on, with all the equipment, and so on. And then we took off. And for some reason or other, I always got picked for some of the -- I was handed an SP band to put on my arm, got handed a billy club, and said my post was down in the lower deck with the troops in the rear of the ship. Well, I didn't think anything of that. So I go down there, and there's all these black fellows are down there, and they are quite jovial and all that. They are sparring and boxing and doing all kind of goofy things. But then, all of a sudden, we were into the Japanese currents. This old ship had twin screws on the back of it. Not only did it pitch, but it also rolled as a result of those twin screws on the back. Well, these guys commenced to get seasick. Well, the crew of the ship, which was Norweigian guys, they were operating the ship; but they had what they called a troop master, a Naval man, Naval officer, who was on the ship. And he was in charge of all the personnel. Even though we had our own officers, he was the boss and troop commander. Anyway, these guys commenced to get seasick, and they had put 55-gallon drums out in the middle of the floor for them to upchuck in, anticipating that this was going to happen, and it sure as heck did. I thought it was rather humorous. I am down there watching these poor guys get sick and vomit all over each other and so on. And at 4 o'clock when my tour of duty -- no. At 8 o'clock when my tour of duty was up, I make my way up the ladder; and the minute I parted the blackout curtains and smelled that fresh air, it hit me. Boy, I made a beeline for the side of the ship, because for about three days I was sick as a dog. And I wasn't the only one. There were some fellows that got so sick that they had to take them off the ship when we got to Pearl Harbor. They were really sick. It took me about three days to get over it; but once it passed, I never was bothered again. And we sailed two or three times after that, got tied up in a typhoon on our way to China. Didn't bother me a lick. Didn't bother me a bit. And it's funny, like you are inoculated or immune or something. One time was enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any trouble between the blacks and whites then?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: No, there wasn't. There wasn't. This is before Truman's time when he mixed them. But they were by themselves. We'd go back, and we used to have boxing matches. And they, of course, all thought they were Joe Lewis or Sugar Ray Robinson or something like that. They had a couple of guys who were rather good. Daily entertainment was to go back there and challenge somebody and get up on the deck or up on the top of the hold, the cargo hold, which was covered with canvas in kind of like a ring, and go back there and box. And I was dumb enough to do it because as a kid, I had hung around with -- Amateur boxing was big when I was a kid, you know? For five bucks, which was big money if you could go three rounds in an amateur boxing show. But yeah, we mixed with them. They stayed pretty much back there, but I'd go back all the time because where I come from, I knew lots of -- we had lots of kids on our team, black kids on the team at that time. In those days you called them colored kids. But we were -- went to school together, did everything together. But we stopped in Pearl Harbor. We went over there unescorted, which really kind of surprised me that we went from California to Pearl Harbor unescorted. And there were still loose Japanese submarines around, guys who hadn't been chased away. And we spent three days at Pearl Harbor just waiting for a cargo -- or for a convoy because from there on -- it was still '43 -- no, '44, early '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that early '44 or '45?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Forty-four.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Forty-four, okay.

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Because -- We stopped at Pearl, and we picked up a convoy there; and then we went on, on our way. We stopped at Enewetak. We stopped at Quadulane and Ulythe, Pelalieu. And eventually, as we reached the Philippines, we docked at an at a little, real small island called Calicoan, which is right in the southern tip of the island of Samar, which is one of the bigger islands in the Philippine chain. But we weren't allowed to get off the ship unless you wanted to jump over the side and take a bath or swim because we had no fresh water on the ship for bathing. They had it for drinking, but you couldn't -- I was on duty late one night, and I saw an officer, one of the Norweigian ship's crew. It was probably 2 o'clock in the morning. And we sailed along with no lights or anything like that. It was under strict blackout curtains, no running lights or anything. And I see this fellow come out of a door with a towel and soap and all this stuff, and I said, "Holy mackerel." So I looked in there. It was a shower. Boy, I scooted back down to my hold and got my sea bag and got a bar of soap and a towel and went right back up there. In the middle of the night, I took a fresh water shower, which was great because 40 days without anything other than salt water, you know -- We had salt water soap, but that left a crust on you. And, of course, if you are out in the ocean, you pass through a lot of clouds. You could look in all directions and see clouds. And under those clouds, it's raining like the Dickens. And if you sail through one, you are going to get a nice shower. And we kind of take advantage of that. Of course, you didn't have to worry about it no women around. We'd just take off our clothes and take a shower. Anyway, when we stopped at Ulythe, I will never forget that. There were ships as far as you could see on the horizon that were getting ready to go to Okinawa, up that way, make those two landings up there at Okinawa and -- what the heck is the other one?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Iwo Jima?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Iwo Jima and Okinawa, yeah. Aircraft carriers solid from horizon to horizon, every kind of ship imaginable, aircraft carriers, battleships, everything. We stayed there for a day or so, and then we sailed on, went to Pelalieu, stopped there. Of course, we couldn't get off the ship other than to jump over the side. And you look at that and you could say, "Where in the heck is the land?" Because the land wasn't much more than three feet above the water. And make you wonder, what the heck? But you could see a few buildings over in there, but you are out. You are usually tied up quite a ways out. They'd assign you a berth to drop anchor. And we got into the Philippines there, and we disembarked. Quite a bit going on there at the time. And we were only there for, maybe, a week or two; and they split our battalion. And I happened to be in Company B; and they took us about 250 men, put us on an LCT and shipped us out, threw a bunch of plywood on there and stuff and supplies. And we didn't know where in the heck we were going. But the rest of our battalion stayed there. So we take off down through Leyte Gulf, probably 75 miles away on this LCT, 250 guys in the company. We have our company commander and platoon chiefs and all that sort of thing. Didn't have a doctor. We had a corpsman. And we traveled on down and go up into Leyte Gulf, which is a large body of water. That's where the Philippine invasion was made when MacArthur returned to the Philippines. That's where the first invasion was made. And we ended up on Samar, but 75 miles down the bay right across from the provincial capital of Leyte, which was a town or a city called Tacloben. Not much of a city. A few permanent buildings, but there weren't a whole lot of them, but there was an air strip there. And that's where the initial invasion was when MacArthur returned. There were about three beaches along there on Leyte where they went ashore. It was kind of an interesting sight to ride along there and see all these palm trees with no tops on them. There were just these sticks everywhere, hundreds or thousands of sticks that had been palm trees; but when the invasion occurred, they just blew the Dickens out of them. But the shoreline of the airport, which was right on the water, practically, was just littered or piles upon piles of airplanes, wrecked airplanes, where they bulldozed them off of the runway. As they crashed on the runway, they bulldozed them into the water, just ours, Japanese, all kinds, just bulldozed them into the water to clear the runways so that the planes could land. But we then went across the bay, and there was another outfit already there that had come up from New Guinea, the 101st Construction Battalion. We were the 32nd Special Battalion. We had kind of a -- I think we could have done anything because we had all kinds of skills in the men there. We had heavy equipment operators and diesel repairmen, powder men, electricians. Heck, they could do anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Well, us, the young fellows, we were -- we were just helpers. They needed young, strong guys. I ended up probably being the youngest guy in our -- in our company because we were detached from our battalion. We didn't know what the heck they were doing. They were -- we never saw them again. Never saw the rest of our battalion. I was a winch driver. I learned to operate the winches, which is rather -- one of the more skillful jobs. You'd better be reliable to do that job, you know. But I did a little bit of anything that needed to be done. A lot of our time was just marking time there. We knew, I guess -- I think what was in store for us was, once they made the -- if, in fact, they made the landing on the mainland of Japan, this was a big staging area. They had built a fleet hospital there and a big boat pool. And we went out and handled cargo from ships to shore. And I remember an Australian task group came in there before they went to Borneo. The Aussies made three landings in Borneo, and we were involved in them. The United States was involved in them. But they made an invasion at Brunei Bay and Terracan Island and Ghalib Bapan was the three landing spots in Borneo. But the Aussies came into our place and got a lot of ammunition and that sort of thing. We handled -- we handled ammunition. And they had these warehouses, floating cement warehouses. They were anchored way out. They wouldn't let them into the inner harbor because if they blew up, why, they'd probably take some other ships with them. And they wouldn't allow the big tankers that were carrying aviation fuel in there either. They had to tie up way out. And if we had to to go out and work one of those ships, heck, it was probably a five or six hour ride in an LCT to get out there. And they would feed us, of course, on the ship; and we'd stay there until we would finish the job, and then we'd go back. Plus we, somehow or another -- I don't know how they acquired this thing. We had a giant crane mounted on pontoons. Pontoons are nothing more than square steel cubes, airtight cubes. And they'd hook them together, and you could make a big barge out of them. Well, we had this giant crane, probably handled 75, 80 tons. It was probably the biggest crane east of Pearl Harbor. And we were given that thing to operate, and some of the older men, the chiefs, and some of those fellows who had handled big ships in the United States, why, they -- but I got on that crew. And that was an experience. Oh, boy. We'd go out and unload things from -- one day, we had to do a crash boat. Crash boats were like a torpedo boat, a speedy boat that could go to crash sites and get there in a hurry, very fast, a lot like a torpedo boat. But we lifted the darn thing up. And as we lifted it up, it was a deck cargo on a giant tanker full of gasoline, I guess. And it was sitting up on the deck. And we lifted that thing up and backed away with the barge, and we had two diesel engines on the back of the barge that propelled it. And we started to let it down and had a giant -- we had a giant hook and shiv to pick that thing up. It was way heavier than we could handle because the front of our barge was probably three feet in the water. As we picked up on it, the barge went down. We got it up just high enough to clear the edge of the ship, and then we backed away and started to let it down. It was a brand new boat, nice looking thing. And we started letting it down. And we had a gasoline engine running our winch on the back that powered the hooks and so on. And the boom couldn't swing. It was stiff. It was mounted, but you could move the barge in order to go side to side. The fellow operating the winch -- a young guy like myself; in fact, he was from Cleveland -- he kind of panicked. As we started down, the thing started to getting away from him; and he stepped on the brake, which was what he shouldn't have done. Well, that parted the cable, snapped the cable. And the thing started going through the shivs, and the boat, of course, went into the water. And the great big block and tackle fell on top of the boat, smashed the top of it in. But the big wave action made a suni or -- like we just had. And our barge, of course, did that. And I will never forget our chief. He was an electrician, so he didn't know much about that, but he looked like Captain Bligh. He is standing on the back of the barge back by the winch, standing there in his yellow -- he had one of these yellow foul weather suits, the yellow things. They still have them. He is standing there; and, boy, this big wave comes back and takes Chief Soldiers out to sea, washed him over the side. He is out there flopping around. We, as young guys, we thought that was funnier than the Dickens. Well, you think you are infallible anyway. (END OF CD 1, SR02. BEGIN CD 2, SR03)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The water?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah, we got him out of the water. A lot of interesting things happened there. We were coming along one night, one month, early one morning in the fog, and we can hear voices. And, of course, we recognized them as Americans. What the heck is that? So we go over there. We had an LCT. It's a landing craft with the gate in the front. You have seen lots of them. They'd hold a truck, maybe. And we had one, and we used it as kind of a taxi to take us wherever we needed to go around the bay there. And we go over there, and here sits a PT boat. What the heck? What are these guys here? They had run on the reef. The tide was was out. They were running -- they were taking officers from the carriers and the battleships into a recreation area on the shore. And I guess they didn't observe -- you had, kind of, road maps because there are reefs in there; and when the tide's out, you better not go in there. And they'd get those things going like the Dickens, you know. They'd travel like crazy. Here they had run on the reef. A couple of us jumped over the side and went down and looked underneath. And, boy, the propellers, were just -- they were rosebuds. They were all squeezed out. So we had to give them a line and tow them back to the beach. I never knew what happened to that. But we had a lot of funny experiences like that, where PT boats -- guys would buzz us with their B-51s, Army guys. We'd be riding along, bobbing along in the waves, and they'd get right behind us, right down on the water. And you couldn't hear them it until they roared over the top, and it scared the Dickens right out of you. Of course, there were no jets in those days. There were P-38s and P-40s, all kind of Navy planes. Being a little bit of an airplane nut, I taught myself to recognize aircraft by sound because every airplane, if you pay close enough attention, has its own peculiar sound. I used to -- guys were always challenging me because they thought, "You can't do that." And I got fooled one time. We'd be in our tent, and a plane would go roaring over. And a guy would say, "Okay, Mac, what was that?" And I would say, "Well, that was a such and such." Well, I had a real close friend who knew them by vision, but by sight, but he hadn't paid that much attention to the sounds. And he went out, and I told him, I said, "Well, that was a B-51." And we used to bet on it. You know, they would bet against me. Hey, I made a lot of money because I tried to cover everything. They didn't realize I could do that. But he comes in, and he says, "You're wrong." I said, "Whoa. I'm wrong?" So we went out. And pretty soon he comes back, and here was a Spitfire. A Spitfire and a B-51 had the same engine. They are about the same size. I had never seen a Spitfire, and they sounded almost the same. During the night an Australian -- this Australian task group had come in with their aircraft carriers and their cruisers. And I don't think they had a battle wagon, battleship. They had a couple cruisers and some destroyers and one or two aircraft carriers. And they put these guys in, and they were flying around. And that was the same group that went to -- They asked for volunteers. They needed some guys, and I volunteered. Another kid and I volunteered. Then they changed their mind and they said, "Well, you might not get back with us. It would be hard to get you back from down there." I wanted to go somewhere. I wanted to see something, see as much as I could anyway. But I didn't get to go. But you know, we -- like I said earlier, I seemed to get a lot of goofy assignments. One day, the company chief came down and said, "Hey, Mac," he said. Everybody called me Mac. And in the Navy, that's kind of the wrong thing to do. You are not supposed to call guys Mac in the Navy. He said, "How about you and John going --" some guy had died in the regular outfit that was back on Calbayog, and they were sending his body to the military cemetery on Leyte, which was full of soldiers who had been killed in the invasion of Leyte the past October. And he says, "I need a couple guys to go over and go with this burial, somebody from our battalion. So we went down and got in the LCT and rode across the bay to Leyte. And, lo and behold, there is another LCT there and some soldiers, four or five soldiers, a couple guys; and they had a casket, a wooden casket. And we loaded it into a weapons carrier and took off through the jungle. And, boy, all of a sudden, we break out of jungle into a big open area, I mean, a giant field that had been leveled, all the palm trees and everything. As far as the eye could see were white crosses. And that really opened my eyes to the reality of what was going on, or what -- And, of course, we had to -- they had already prepared a spot. And we had to take the body down there and take the casket down there. And they had a crew. The Army had a crew that ran the cemetery, and that's all they did. And so they were ready for it. Boy, that was an experience. Plus, while we were at Pearl Harbor, we were tied up in the canal that leads into Pearl Harbor. And a ship came this there one day. In fact, it was a big, brand, spanking new aircraft carrier, the one -- what was -- the Shangri-la came in while we were tied up there on its first cruise. Boy, when it went through the canal, it raised the water so that it tore ships away from their moorings and everything. Ships were drifting around that carrier after it went by. And it was brand spanking new. Anyway, this old cargo vessel came in and tied up in front of us. And we walked down and, lo and behold -- we couldn't figure out, what the heck? They brought these, what they called, elephant trucks. They were like a semi. Around here they carry horses in them. A bunch of them showed up, and then all of a sudden, this truckload of Marines get out with full battle gear and shotguns and machines guns and everything else. So, what the heck? Let's get down there. So we walked down to see what was going on. So they commenced. They had a whole bunch of Japanese prisoners. They were bringing them back to Pearl Harbor. A lot of them were stretcher case. They carried them down a gangplank. A lot of them were walking wounded. And they were the sorriest looking bunch of guys. That was my first experience of seeing the enemy, seeing those poor souls. And, boy, do they look like they were scared to death because there are these Marines standing around with shotguns and everything. They, obviously, had a prison there for them. They loaded them on, loaded them in these trucks and took them away. But they were a sorry bunch of guys. They had been in the cargo hold of this old cargo ship. It had a hole through the side of it where you could look right through the ship. It had a hole through it. You could -- just like two windows, a big hole through there. When it was empty, of course, it's riding high out of the water. And they probably had their bilge pumps going. But it had come back. I asked one of the crewmen, I says, "Where are these guys coming from?" "They are coming from Luzon." That's where -- the Army had gone up there. And that's where Manila is up on the mainland. The main city of the Philippines in the middle of the capital is up there on Luzon. There was a lot of heavy fighting up in there. And that was still going on when we were in Samar. We only -- the only thing we saw in Samar were mock-up operations, and they were being handled by the Filipino guerrillas. And on an almost daily basis, a platoon or a squad of them would pass our camp and go up into the mountains. And a couple days later, they'd come back with a half a dozen Japanese prisoners. They had them all chained together. And they were half starved, you know. They had been up in there. They had escaped or gone up into the hills to -- you know, we'd see that, maybe, a couple days a week. We'd see them bring guys down out of there. There was no organized resistance in that area at the time. That was an eye opener, to go to that military cemetery on Leyte and see. Plus, there was a field hospital there, too; and I volunteered to go over there. One day, a big -- great big white hospital ship came in. And I had two real close friends who were signalmen. They had gone to signalmen school. And, in fact, I just -- we just had a meeting. We got together, three of us, a couple years ago out in Oregon. One of them lives out there, and the three of us got together. One fellow was from -- well, he was from West Virginia, and the other one was from Iowa. And we were real close. We were very -- we did everything together. And they had a signal shack up on the mountain with a light, and they could talk to all the ships in the harbor. They couldn't talk by radio, but they did everything by light. And they -- anyway, we'd go over. This big hospital ship came, this big, white hospital ship with a big Red Cross on the side of it; and they asked for volunteers. So we went over to Leyte. And here they were evacuating that field hospital. So we went back. They took us back in the jungle, and there was tents back there. And these guys had been wounded in the invasion, in the Leyte invasion. Boy, some of them had been there for a good while. And our job was to stretcher -- help them carry stretchers out of there down to the beach and put them on landing craft, took them out to this hospital ship. Boy, that was another eye opener, all these guys -- I think. I look at that and I say, "Boy, but for something, there go I." Those guys were just like me. I could be one of them very easily. Boy. But we spent the summer there, a good bit of that summer. And that's -- during that time is when the atom bomb was dropped on Hiroshima. And we were -- these guys up on the -- my friends up there operating the light were the first guys to hear it because they picked it up from the ships. And we had an Armed Forces Radio station on Leyte, and it had a little better -- it would pick it up across the bay. We would listen to Harry James and Glenn Miller and Tommy Dorsey. They'd play music at night, and if you were lucky enough to have a radio -- One of the fellows in our outfit who was a good radio man. He had gone over to Leyte, gotten in one of the bombers that had been pushed into the bay, took the radio out, brought it back, hooked it up and had speakers up in the palm trees; and we could all appreciate the Armed Forces Radio station from this aircraft radio. That was a -- darned thing could pick up anything. But he was good at that. And then we get to, once that happened, why --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction when they heard about the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: There was a lot -- we were out -- we were out on a big tanker out in the middle of the bay. We had done a job out there. And, boy, all of a sudden, the ships all started blowing their horns and raising all kind of Cain. Some guys were firing in the air and that sort of thing, but there was lots of screaming and yelling and hollering. And that was the end of hostilities. That was it. Of course, we were around there for some time, and that's when we learned that the GI bill had been adopted, had been passed. And boy, I, of course, had no -- no thought of going to college unless I would, maybe, do something with an athletic scholarship or something of that nature. But the day I got my draft notice, I was talking with a fellow who had come to Wellsville trying to recruit guys. I guess he was looking down the road for after the war to get guys to come to Ohio Wesleyan to play football. I don't know whether, somehow or other, somebody sicked him on me. I was sitting in his car talking with him when the mailman handed me my report notice. "Congratulations, you have been selected by a panel of your friends and neighbors." Anyway, but a good experience for an 18-year-old kid. Anyway, we, once the war was -- that part of it was over and the fighting was, supposedly stopped, it wasn't long after that that the Indianapolis was sunk. And it was headed for Leyte Gulf at the time. And we -- that's the one that the Japanese submarine sank that got the captain court-martialed. And later they kind of cleared him. But anyway, they then commenced to send troops home. They had to get guys back home. And they set up this point system. Of course, we had a lot of older men in our outfit, these skilled guys. And many of them were married, and they had points for that sort of thing. And they set up a point system. You got so many points for the length of time were you in the service and so many points for whatever rank you had achieved. If you were married, da da da da, you got points. Of course, the young guys didn't have any points. We didn't have doodly. At least, we didn't think we did. And they started shipping those guys home. They called it the Magic Carpet. That was the name of the operation to get guys out of the Pacific to get them home, the Magic Carpet. And, of course, at the same time, they needed to do something with the Japanese. So they took all of the young fellows in our company. The older guys got -- well, they either stayed there, or they got a way to go home. If there were any ships going home, they'd take as many as they could and send them back to the States. Well, they took all of us young fellows and put us together and sent us to China. And we -- of course, we had no more older guys. All the young fellows, they put us on an old APA, the 133 Beckham. I will never forget that. The name of the old ship that we went across the Pacific was the Japara, J-a-p-a-r-a, the motor ship Japara. And it had been built in Germany, in Homburg, I think. And the crewmen who were Norweigian guys, they didn't speak much English; but we'd try to talk with them anyway. Anyway, we were sent to China. This was on a Naval vessel, a Naval cargo ship, an attack -- one of the ones that they had the landing craft on, and they had Marines or soldiers on. Well, they loaded us up on that thing, and we took off for China. We didn't know where in the heck we were going. We were just going someplace. We spent about two days loading up our equipment, and away we went. Some of the guys got seasick again. It didn't bother me. A lot of us were immune at that point. We sailed north. And as we were sailing north out of -- come out of Leyte Gulf and took off on straight north. And, of course, you know where you are going because you know where the sun sets and where the sun gets up, comes up in the morning. I hated to sleep down in the hold because the body smell was not too good. And I would sleep out on the deck. And, boy, you get all those guys down in there, and wow. Anyway, I would sleep out on the deck with my poncho and whatever I could get under a landing craft and lay there. I will never forget this one night I am out there, and the weather got progressively worse. The wind kicked up, and I can hardly keep my poncho on me, and it got kind of cold. And I wake up in the morning, and the sun's coming up on the wrong side of the ship. I said, "What the heck is this?" During the night, we had turned around. So I got hold of one of the crew of the ship, and I said, "What the heck's going on?" I said, "We are going the wrong direction. Last night when we -- the sun went down, it was on the left side of the ship, and here it is on the left side again." He said, "Well, there was a big storm up north of us, and we are turned around. We are just killing time now. We are going to steam south for a little while." And then, until we turned around -- well, later on that day, we turned around and took off back north again. And, lo and behold, we continued to travel north, and we get into a typhoon. And in 1945, this is. That typhoon literally wrecked Okinawa, just destroyed everything. It was a whopper. And we continued to steam. We are sailing right out. I thought, "What the heck are we doing?" It's getting progressively worse. And the daggone waves got up to where they are 30 feet high, you know. The ship would raise up, and then it would drop down and vroom, the bow pound. This is a big ship, a victory ship, would go under the water. You would stand back under the (inaudible). The waves were running down the stacks, and it's rolling. And I thought, "Jesus, criminy. This is the end of it for us." Anyway, we spent five days in that dang thing. We had a destroyer escort leading us up front, a little ship, a lot smaller than a destroyer. Sometimes you could only see the top of the mast on it sticking up out of the water. The wind blowing, you couldn't -- you couldn't -- everything had to be done holding on. You ate standing up holding on. And you got in your sack at night, you had to hold on because that dang thing is rolling and bucking, and the anchors are clapping against the side. And the screws would come out of the water in the rear and go nuts when they came out of the water. They'd just go wild, you know, because there is no resistance. You'd go back down. We spent five days in that. By now, we are into the Yellow Sea, and the darned thing had been mined. And during the night, there up on the bridge was 25 millimeters shooting at these mines floating around in the water. Every now and then, they'd hit one, you know, big things with spines sticking out. They'd hit one, and there would be a gigantic explosion. Of course, you could hit one of them very easily because they were -- We stopped at Okinawa. We just tied up there for a little bit. And, boy, there were ships up on the beach 100, 150 yards up on the beach, big tankers laying on their sides. You could see that there was a lot of devastation there. We weren't there very long, and we took off and went on to China. We were headed mainly for a town up just opposite the Korean peninsula, what is called the Shandong peninsula up in Northern China. There were two cities up there settled by the Germans back at the turn of the century. One was Tientsin. It was up north. We went up there first and put half of our guys ashore there. And we couldn't -- we couldn't go up the Yang -- the river there, and we had to tie up on what was called the Tanggu bar right at the mouth of the river. And we put them on barges, and they took off and went into town. We couldn't see the city or anything. As soon as we got them unloaded, we sailed down around the peninsula to another town called Qingdao. It's called Tsingtao now. They have changed all the names, like Beijing. They have changed the names of all the cities. Those were two major cities up in that area, and the Japanese had occupied those since 1938. They had their families in there, and they were well ensconced in there, been there forever. And, of course, the place is Qingdao, where they dumped us off, didn't look Chinese. It looked more European. The buildings, the big stone buildings, they didn't have any temples. There were a couple of them around, but mainly you thought you you were in Europe because it had been settled by the Germans. The Japanese Navy had a suicide boat base there. We went ashore and took -- we were able there to sail right into the docks. They had rather nice, big stone docks from wars and so on. We could tie up right in there. And that was part of our job there was to handle the cargo. Anything that the Navy or the Marine Corps needed coming in there, we handled it, because many of the merchant ships that were carrying that stuff wouldn't allow the Chinese aboard. They didn't want the Coolies, and so on, aboard their ships. And our job was to operate the machinery. And, of course, a lot of the Marines had to do the work, which they resented the heck out of because they were infantry, and they had come over there from Okinawa and Iwo Jima. A lot of them had been in much of the fighting over there, and they felt that was beneath them. But anyway, that was -- The city was a rather big city, a rather nice town. Of course, the Japanese had let it go to pot. And there was a lot of -- a lot of poverty there. That was really an eye opener to see the poverty of the Chinese people who the Japanese had really persecuted since 1938. They had been there a long time. And they had built apartment houses. Heck, a lot of them had their families in there and everything. Our first billeting, the first place we were housed, it was in a Japanese suicide boat base. They confiscated all the automobiles in town, and they built these little speedboats. They were only, maybe, 12 or 15 feet long, and they had an automobile engine in them, any kind of engine they could get. And they had a direct drive screw, and the pilot sat in a little hole, a little square hole right in the very back end. And then they would mount a big charge, I guess, up in the front of bombs or dynamite or something. And the idea was to ram it into the side of a ship, which they did in some instances. But that was their training base. And they had dozens of these little boats in caves. And some of them, they took the trailer -- took the automobiles and made trailers out of the wheels and so on. Each boat was mounted on a trailer, and they could push it down into the water. This was -- we thought it was great fun. They had a great big barracks there, and we lived in that barracks. And we experienced the Japanese bath house. They have a separate building with a big pool in it and all these little wooden tubs. You build a fire in the thing, and it warms up the water, and you could take a bath. Plus the -- Anyway, I had a friend from Kentucky that and he and I had been together for a long time. And John knew a lot about cars. Well, he and I go over to where the boats were, and we fiddle around and fiddle around; and he determines that this one looks like it's got everything in it. Well, in the meantime, we had been in one of their out buildings, and we got down in the basement. And here, the floor was covered with automobile batteries. So he takes a wire and goes around and checks, and he finds one with some juice in it. Well, we cart that thing down there and put it in this boat, hook it up, got some gasoline. Gasoline was plentiful, of course. Hooked it up -- vroom. It had a 36 Ford engine, V-8 engine, a little dingy boat. We got that thing in the water, and we'd ride around out in the bay in it. In November, it's colder than the Dickens. We had heavy parkas on. We were out there. Probably a wonder we didn't get shot down. We go out in the harbor and, my God, there is a battleship out there and an aircraft carrier. And we are out there riding around amongst those guys, and the guys up on deck are all yelling at us. And we didn't have brains enough to have a flag even. There was a land swell. The water will do this. We are scooting along showing off, you know. He is back there driving. I am riding up in the front. We scooted off the top of this wave, and we go in nose first. Man, that stalled out the engine. And we are bobbing away out there, and we can't get the darned thing started because it's flooded. We had a broom, so we rode ourselves back into the beach with the broom. That was something. Those are the funny things you remember a lot of. Qingdao was an interesting, rather large city. They had a big race track there for horse racing. And they had a surrender ceremony out at the race track. And the Marines every day would conduct a parade. Mainly, it was a show of strength because the Japanese are still there. The Chinese Communists were there. One night, we brought in the Chinese Nationalist 8th Army from down in the Salween. They came in. We had a Marine Corps in there and ourselves. And all these guys are armed all the time. In the city, in downtown, they are milling around. And, of course, the Chinese are trying to get businesses open to make the Yankee dollar and that sort of thing. It was kind of dangerous. There would be shooting every night, you know, because the Chinese nationalists and the Communists were kind of at loggerheads. Submersion pilots were kidnapped. There was a little airport out there, and some marine dive bomber pilots were kidnapped, and I guess they finally -- I don't know who, probably the Communists, I would guess, that they wanted to take over. But we had to -- they had a surrender ceremony out at the race track. We went out. And they had all these Japanese soldiers in platoons standing out there at attention. And their commanding officer, I guess it would be, he surrendered to the Marines. They were the hierarchy of the Marine Corps. I think Lemuel Shepherd, who later became the commandant of the Marine Corps was -- we were attached to the 6th Marine Division. They were in there, probably three regimens; I think the 29th Marine Regimen, the 19th Marine Regimen and, I think, the 22nd or something like, that were in there. And most of them had come over from Okinawa and Iwo Jima and that sort of thing. They had this big, formal surrender ceremony. And we had our tanks and that sort of thing. Every day there would be a kind of a parade of vans and so on through the streets just to kind of let them know we are there and to keep them under control. But we were there. Then, lo and behold, we organized another football team because all these young guys -- and had no equipment. So it was supposed to be touch football. And they had a stadium there in town, probably a soccer stadium, because there was a university in town. And we used to go down to the university to play basketball. They had a gymnasium there. I don't think there was any classes or anything going on because Japanese weren't about to do that. But we -- each of the Marine regimens had a team and we had a team, and we would play touch football. Well, it wasn't much touch involved. It was brutal. No wonder more guys didn't get hurt. But we'd go out there and play. We had, on Thanksgiving Day we had the Rice Bowl Game, we called it. We played one of the Marine regimens. Of course, the Marine officers, many of them were college guys. And they acted as officials. The ones who didn't want to play, they would officiate the games. That was one of our entertainments, as well as all kind of funny things to occupy yourself with. But it was kind of a dangerous place in those days because all these guys were armed, and these Chinese Communists, they are walking around, and they got granades hanging on them. And they've got these big Mauser guns strapped to their side. And they were very -- man, they were mean looking, you know. We unloaded a lot of ships there. A lot of Old Liberties came in with -- well, when they brought the 8th Army in there, the Chinese from down in -- they came in under the cover of darkness. They brought them in at night. And the poor guys had been down in the tropics, and it's colder than heck, and they weren't equipped for that sort of thing. And, man, I thought, "What the heck?" They'd huddle around together. And we were unloading gasoline and kerosene, all kind of fuel oil and things like that, for the Marine base out there, the airfield. And these Chinese guys, they would go over and stab a hole in one of these drums, you know, at night when nobody was around; and they'd get a can and get a can of kerosene. Of course, then they'd stuff some rags back in there. They wanted to build a fire to keep themselves warm. Why, you couldn't blame them. The Chinese, the Coolies, did a lot of the work, the labor work. We just operated the equipment and supervised. Our job was mainly a supervisory thing to -- even the Marines that worked under us. They didn't like that, but they -- We had a black Marine group who had been ammunition handlers on Okinawa. I got to know a couple of them pretty well, and they would tell me some of the stories. I think I was probably the youngest guy to be given my own -- my own, what we called a gang, 14 guys, and myself was 15. And I was to -- I kind of supervised them. You know, they'd tell me what needed to be done, the officers would, and it was my job to get it done. I had at least 14 guys under me. We had a truck, and we'd travel around by truck. It was kind of -- I remember the first night we came in there. The Marines had been in there ahead of us. And we are going through the streets, and the street -- the wires for the telephone wires and the wires are all hanging down. And we got these big 8 by 8 -- these big trucks. And, holy cow, these guys are driving along, and the street light wires are hanging down, and we are catching those things and tearing them down. Boy it was a mess. And we'd go by this schoolhouse, red brick schoolhouse, big two-story, maybe three-story thing, and it's smoldering. It burned, obviously, during the night. Well, we had learned later that the Marines had been in there. They had billeted in there. They were living in it. And they had a fire in there to keep warm, and they caught the darn place on fire and burned the schoolhouse down. Oh, kid. That was all kind of -- That was an experience to be in the same town in those days. The poverty and life. Life was so cheap. I remember one day, early one morning, I am standing out on the deck of the ship that we were working, and I could hear -- and it was foggy, real foggy. And I could hear this choo, choo, choo, choo, choo. And I thought, "What the heck is that noise?" And I kept listening. I could see -- pretty soon, I see something coming through the fog. And here it's a little tugboat, a little -- one long tugboat pulling a great, big, flat barge. Now, what in the heck is this? Chug, chugging along. And as it got closer and closer and passed by, the whole deck of that barge right out to the very edge of the gunnels with no guardrails or anything are men standing, all standing there. And they are taking them from one side of the bay to the other to work, I guess, Chinese Coolies. And they all stand there. Normally, when you get a bunch of men together, they are going to be talking, but they are all just standing there like statues. And I watched that thing pass by and disappear into the fog, and I am thinking, "Holy cow. Those are human beings in there, people just like us." One day they were bringing freight cars, little four-wheeled buggy-type freight cars. They had a railroad over there. And we were putting 55-gallon drums of gasoline, picking them out of the ship, putting them down there, and they were on the ground. And they would -- they would put them in the -- take the straps loose, and we would go back up and get another one. As soon as it got full, they would all get behind it and push. They didn't have an engine. They all just got behind it and pushed it. But they weren't very big. The freight cars were narrow gauge, I guess, only had four wheels on it, not the big trucks like we are used to with two wheels on each truck. And I will never forget this. One man, when they pushed it up against the -- one of the drums, rolls off. Well, a 55-gallon drum of anything is plenty of weight. It falls right on this guy, smashes the Dickens out of him. And I am standing up there, and I am looking at that, and I am sure my eyes are bugging out. And they all -- the rest of them just kind of looked at him and walked away, just walked away. The drum rolled off to the side, and I stood there and watched; and here this guy's laying there on the ground writhing around. Pretty soon a truck comes up, an old flatbed truck, charcoal burning truck, had a flat on the back, burned charcoal. And a couple of guys go on out, picked him up, throw him up on the bed of the truck, and away they go. And boy, I am thinking, "Holy, jumping Jehovah. And, of course, you'd see kids, dead kids in the street. A kid died of starvation or whatever, he would be in the street. And, eventually, they -- the streets were just crowded with people all the time just milling around. It was kind of -- I always felt that it was kind of dangerous to go down there. But we did it anyway. We'd go down and go in the stores and -- This fellow from Kentucky one day and I decide well, we are going to go explore a little bit. So we take off. We walk up the road, and here we come to a compound. Everything's walled in. Everything's walled in and had cement on the tops of the walls with broken glass on up there so if you jumped up on the wall to jump over, you are kind of in trouble. But there were some nice homes there. A lot of what they call White Russian people lived there, because we are up near Manchuria, you know? We are up in there. And we come across this compound, and we walked through this gate and go in there; and here's, obviously, a military base but nobody around. Obviously, Japanese military headquarters. Well, heck. We didn't have guns or sidearms or anything. We are just -- so I -- there is a stairway going up to the second floor. So I said, "Let's go up there and see what's up there." So we go up the stairs, get to the tops of the stairs, shove the door open; and here it's a barracks. It's a radio headquarters, Japanese radio headquarters, had all these radios in there that they could probably talk to the mainland. And these guys look, and they see us; and they jump out of their bunks, and they all stand rigidly at attention and here are a couple of daggone American sailors who don't know what the heck they are doing. They all jumped down out of their bunks and stood at attention, you know? And we walked in, and we tried to make them understand that we wanted a Japanese flag. And they, of course, are nodding their head and smiling and bobbing and weaving. And we are acting like we are running, and we are drawing a picture of a flag, and they are grinning. I think I we finally got one, but I don't think we got one from there. But anyway, it could have been dangerous. They couldn't -- they would be -- the ones in town, if you had met Japanese soldiers, they would always step aside and bow when you went by. They bowed to the Americans. The city itself was -- could have been a very pretty town, very beautiful city. Had some nice, big governmental buildings in the downtown area. Of course, the park areas were just full of garbage and and litter. They had let it go to the Dickens. Then we stayed there. And I came home in February.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was this? Would that be February '46?

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Victor W. McIntire
sp.p: We were there for I don't know how many months. And I found out by accident. Well, when I first went in -- I came from a large family. And one of the fellows in town told me, he said, "Well, when you get inducted, tell them you want an allotment," because I came from a large family and had a lot of brothers and sisters. And my folks operated their own mom-and-pop-type business. And they said, "You send some of your pay home, and the government will match it." I thought, "Well, heck that's not a bad --" So I did. And, lo and behold, I received an allotment. I was one of nine kids. So part of my pay was matched by the government, and my folks would receive a monthly check. Well, lo and behold, that was worth ten points. And I was with this one friend in the chaplain's office. He worked in the chaplain's office. And he -- we were talking about the points. And the chaplain says, "Well, you have got so many points if you had an allotment." I said, "Well, gee whiz, I have an allotment." So, I go to the company office, and the guy says, "Yeah." Heck, I just figured I am like the rest of the guys. And, lo and behold, I have got ten extra points, which made me eligible to go home. And so -- but once you applied or once they found you could go home, it took awhile to get transportation because they sent guys home whatever way they could. They didn't make any special -- Well, they did later on; but at that time, the early guys, they -- if there were a couple bunks on a ship that was going back to the States, they'd take them. Well, I went out one day and got aboard a destroyer, and they had room for 99 guys. I thought, on a destroyer, where in the heck are they going to get room? A destroyer is not that big. But they would sleep in shifts. Well, I was the last name on the list because of my lateness of finding my points, finding those extra ten points. So they took 99 guys and sent me back to the beach. Well, I had to go back and wait, to sit around and wait. And pretty soon, they say, "Well, we have got another ship's going back to the States, a CBE. It's a baby flat top." Well, it didn't arrive. It went somewhere else. A couple days later, well, the Wilkesboro, which was a light cruiser, it's going back. So I go out to the Wilkesboro. They take you out in a little boat out to the ship because they couldn't come into the wharf. Now, the Wilkesboro is not going home. They send you over to the Springfield. So finally, I get on the Springfield, another light cruiser; and that's how I got home. Took us 18 days to come back. And we got into another -- another daggone storm. The ship went wild. It just bucked and carried on, not all the way, but for several days we were in heavy, heavy seas. And we are headed in to California, to San Francisco. And, lo and behold, there was some kind of a dock strike or railroad strike, so they diverted us down to the Wilmington down in San Pedro down at LA, and we went down there. And then from there, they put us on trains, of course. And I went and came back to Great Lakes Naval Training Station in Chicago, or north of Chicago there, and that's where I was discharged. And, of course, you are on your own once they hand you your mustering out money and with whatever you are carrying. And I got a train from Chicago to Pittsburgh and got a bus from Pittsburgh down to my hometown. (END OF TAPE 2.)
